title: Bitcoin Crypto Stack — secp256k1, SHA-256, Schnorr

questions.question: In Bitcoin code, what does HASH256 (sometimes written SHA256d) mean?
options: SHA256(SHA256(m))
SHA256(m || m)
SHA256(m) truncated to 256 bits
SHA256(SHA1(m))
questions.explanation: HASH256 is the double-SHA256 construction: hash the input with SHA-256 twice.

questions.question: What is a BIP340 x-only public key?
options: A 32-byte x-coordinate with the convention that the corresponding y is even
A 33-byte compressed SEC1 public key (02/03 || x)
A 64-byte (x || y) point encoding without any prefix
A 32-byte secret scalar reduced modulo p
questions.explanation: BIP340 public keys are 32 bytes (x-only) and rely on an even-y convention to remove ambiguity.

questions.question: Which definition matches BIP340 tagged_hash(tag, m)?
options: SHA256(SHA256(tag) || SHA256(tag) || m)
SHA256(tag || m)
SHA256(SHA256(tag || m))
SHA256(m || SHA256(tag))
questions.explanation: Tagged hashing domain-separates contexts by hashing the tag twice and prefixing the message with it.

questions.question: Why does BIP340 require the points P (pubkey) and R (nonce point) to have even y-coordinates?
options: To make encodings unique and avoid malleability from choosing y vs. −y
To ensure the curve equation has exactly one y solution for every x
To make scalar multiplication faster by skipping inversions
To prevent SHA-256 length extension attacks
questions.explanation: For a given x there are two possible y values (y and −y). Fixing an even-y convention makes the mapping unique.

questions.question: In BIP340 verification, what inputs are hashed to form the challenge e?
options: r || pubkey_x || msg (with the BIP0340/challenge tag)
s || pubkey_x || msg (with the BIP0340/challenge tag)
pubkey_x || msg (with the BIP0340/nonce tag)
msg only (with no tag)
questions.explanation: The challenge binds the signature's r, the public key, and the message under the challenge tag.

questions.question: Attack scenario: what happens if the same nonce k is reused to sign two different messages with the same secret key?
options: The secret key can be recovered from the two signatures
Only the public key leaks, but the secret key remains safe
Verification becomes impossible because r is random
Nothing breaks because Schnorr is deterministic
questions.explanation: Nonce reuse makes the signatures algebraically related; an attacker can solve for the secret key.

questions.question: Which checks should a BIP340 verifier do before expensive curve operations?
options: Reject if r ≥ p, s ≥ n, or the x-only pubkey cannot be lifted to a curve point
Reject if r ≥ n, s ≥ p, or the pubkey has odd x
Reject if the signature length is 65 bytes instead of 64 bytes
Reject if the message length is not exactly 32 bytes
questions.explanation: BIP340 uses field size p for r and group order n for s, and requires pubkey lifting to succeed.

questions.question: In Bitcoin transaction signing, which statement is most accurate?
options: Wallets sign a context-specific sighash derived from the transaction, not the txid
Wallets sign the txid directly because it uniquely identifies the transaction
Wallets sign the Merkle root of the block that will contain the transaction
Wallets sign the recipient address string with SHA-256
questions.explanation: The txid is an identifier; the signature commits to a sighash derived from transaction data under protocol rules.
